Legumes (Fabaceae) family, a.k.a. Pea family, is a very large family of flowering plants. Traditionally the Pea Family was divided into several subfamilies, including:

1 Subfamily Faboideae. Familiar western genera include: Astragalus, Dalea, LUPINUS, and Trifolium.
2 Acacias, Mimosas, Mesquites, and Allies (Subfamily Mimosoideae)
3 Peacock Flower Subfamily (Subfamily Caesalpinioideae), includes Palo Verde (Genus Parkinsonia).

Fabaceae is a vast plant family defined by its ecological and economic importance, encompassing trees, shrubs, vines, and herbs that thrive across nearly all climates. Its members are notable for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen through symbiosis with root-dwelling bacteria, a trait that enriches soils and underpins agricultural systems worldwide. The family includes staple food crops such as beans, peas, lentils, and soy, as well as forage plants like alfalfa and clover, making it central to both human diets and livestock feed. Beyond food, Fabaceae provides timber, gums, dyes, and medicinal compounds, while also shaping ecosystems by stabilizing soils and supporting diverse wildlife. Its adaptability and utility have made it one of the most influential plant families in human history and in natural landscapes alike.

Legumes (Fabaceae) family, a.k.a. Pea family, is a very large family of flowering plants. It includes trees, shrubs, and perennial or annual herbaceous plants, which are easily recognized by their fruit (legume) and their compound, stipulate leaves. Fabaceae is the most common family of flowering plants found in tropical rainforests and dry forests of the Americas and Africa. The family is widely distributed, and is the third-largest land plant family in number of species, only behind the Orchidaceae and Asteraceae, with about 765 genera and nearly 20,000 known species, worldwide. Traditionally the Pea Family was divided into three families or subfamilies: Mimosoidea (Mimosa Family), Caesalpinioidea (Senna Family), and the Papilionoidea (Fabaceae)": https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/47122-Fabaceae

Buttercup Tree (Cochlospermum vitifolium), a.k.a Rosa Amarillais (yellow rose) in Spanish, is a flowering tree in the Achiote (Bixaceae) family and the Mallows, Rock-roses, and Allies (Malvales) ORDER. Leaves are deciduous.
Buttercup Tree (Cochlospermum vitifoli) produces 5-petaled, bright yellow flowers that form small, upright clusters rather than long hanging racemes. These flowers appear on mostly bare branches in mid‑January, creating a striking display against the tree’s pale, patchy, almost whitish bark.

"Cochlospermum vitifolium grows up to 12 m (40 ft) tall. Flowers are showy, yellow, solitary, and large, up to 10 cm (4 inches) across. They resemble roses but do not belong to the same family. It inhabits the dry jungles of southern Mexico to Central America from sea level to 1,200 m (3,900 ft) elevation. Its wood produces a yellow-orange dye used for dyeing cotton clothes." https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/132130-Cochlospermum-vitifolium

"Genera In Family: 266 genera; 4025 species worldwide, especially in warm regions."

Mallow and Hibiscus (Malvaceae) family is a large group of flowering plants with more than 240 genera and over 4,000 species. It includes herbs, shrubs, trees, and some woody climbers found in many parts of the world, especially in warm regions. Plants in this family often have soft leaves and young parts covered with star‑shaped hairs. Their tissues release a slimy material when crushed, which is common across the group. The leaves are usually alternate and simple, sometimes divided into lobes, and often have small stipules at the base.
The flowers are one of the easiest ways to recognize the family. They are usually fairly large, and many species have an extra ring of small bracts beneath the main calyx. The stamens are fused into a single column that surrounds the style, which is a key feature of Malvaceae. The fruits vary widely, forming capsules, segmented dry fruits, berries, or nuts depending on the subgroup.
Malvaceae grows in many habitats, including forests, savannas, wetlands, and coastal areas. The family is important to people because it includes plants used for fiber, food, and ornamentals, such as cotton, cacao, hibiscus, and hollyhock. Across this range, the combination of star‑shaped hairs, mucilage, alternate leaves, and flowers with a stamen column helps identify members of the family.
